screens.title: Ansible Inventory Management and Dynamic Inventories
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn how Ansible discovers and organizes your managed nodes, why inventories matter, and how to move from small static lists to dynamic discovery. Inventories are the source of truth for Ansible. We will show you the two common static formats, INI and YAML, how to attach host and group variables so playbooks behave differently per machine, and how variable precedence resolves conflicts when multiple definitions exist. You will also see why dynamic inventories become essential in cloud environments where instances appear and disappear. A concrete example will walk through creating a structured inventory directory with group_vars and host_vars, then running a small playbook that prints resolved variables so you can observe precedence in action. Finally, we will examine a simple dynamic inventory plugin configuration for cloud discovery, and a safety note about securing credentials. By the end you should be able to choose a suitable inventory approach, locate where variables are defined, and diagnose unexpected variable values. Consider how having accurate inventory data could save time when you scale or troubleshoot automation.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Inventory Management
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Ansible Inventory Management

Understand how static and dynamic inventories define hosts, where to put variables, and how Ansible resolves conflicts when multiple values exist.

In this lesson

You will compare INI and YAML inventories, create group_vars and host_vars, run a playbook to observe precedence, and inspect a basic dynamic inventory plugin sample.

Coming up

Hands-on steps that create my_advanced_inventory.ini, group_vars and host_vars, and a display_vars playbook to show resolved values.

⎔
Concept Snapshot
Inventory • Variables • Dynamic
Static Inventory
INI or YAML files you maintain.
Variables
Host, group and global variables.
Dynamic Inventory
Query external sources like cloud APIs.
Explore Key Topics
INI vs YAML
INI is compact; YAML is structured and scales to nested data.
Variables & Precedence
Closer-to-host definitions override broader scope values.
Dynamic Plugins
Plugins let Ansible query clouds and generate inventory on the fly.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives map to hands-on skills you will practice. First, you will configure static Ansible inventory files using both INI and YAML formats so you can choose the right format for your environment. The INI form is quick and readable for small lists, while YAML supports nested data and clearer hierarchy. Second, you will define and use host and group variables to customize task behavior per machine or per group. You will learn where to place host_vars and group_vars files and why they matter. Third, you will understand Ansible's variable precedence — how conflicting definitions resolve — and practice diagnosing surprises using inventory and debug commands. Fourth, you will learn what a dynamic inventory is, why it is useful for cloud environments, and how to run a simple plugin or script to generate inventory automatically. Each objective is paired with a short competence milestone so you can verify you have mastered the skill. By the end, you should be able to choose a static versus dynamic approach, structure variables correctly, and explain why a host-specific value might override a global one.

screens.narratorSegment: These next objectives focus on practical verification and safe practices. screens.title: What is an Ansible Inventory?
screens.narratorSegment: An Ansible inventory is the file or set of files that tell Ansible which machines to manage and how to reach them. At its core an inventory lists hosts, groups them logically, and can attach variables that change playbook behavior. Think of it as a directory and profile system combined: each host is listed and may have a profile made of variables. Static inventories are manually maintained files and are suitable for small or stable infrastructures. They provide control and predictability but become a burden when hosts are frequently created or removed. Dynamic inventories solve that by querying an external source at runtime. A useful mental model is to imagine static inventory as a phonebook you update by hand and dynamic inventory as a live directory that reads from the company's cloud account. A common misconception is to treat inventory only as a list of hostnames; in reality it is also the place where you attach host-specific or group-specific settings that playbooks consume. Example: when you add ansible_user in an all:vars section, that value applies broadly unless a host_vars file defines a different user for a single host. The key takeaway is that inventory controls both discovery and configuration context, so changes to inventory directly affect playbook execution and remote connections. How would your current workflow change if the inventory were always up-to-date?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › What is an Inventory?
Definition

Inventory as directory and profile

An inventory lists hosts, organizes them into groups, and attaches variables so playbooks know how to connect and what values to use.

Key points
  • Hosts are grouped logically for batch operations.
  • Variables may be attached at host, group, or global scope.
  • Static inventory is manual; dynamic inventory is generated at runtime.
Key Takeaway

Inventory determines both which hosts are managed and the configuration context used by playbooks.

Analogy & Example

Analogy: a phonebook where each entry also stores preferences for how to call. Example scenario: one host requires a nondefault SSH port; this is stored as a host variable so playbooks connect correctly.

Common mistake

Assuming inventory is only hostnames. Missing variables or wrong file locations often cause connection or configuration errors.

Check your understanding

If a host has a host_vars file that sets a value and the inventory all:vars sets another, which wins? (Answer: host_vars.)

screens.title: Static Inventory: INI Format
screens.narratorSegment: The INI format is a long-standing, compact way to define static Ansible inventories. It uses bracketed group names, one host per line, and optional inline host variables. It’s ideal for quick setups or environments where nested data is minimal. The example in the chapter shows typical sections: a webservers group, a databases group with a host-specific ansible_port override, and an all:vars section for global variables. Practice reading inline variables carefully: a host line like db1. example. com ansible_port=2222 sets a host-level port that takes precedence over a group or all:vars value. You can also define group-level variables using [groupname:vars] which apply to members of that group. A concrete demonstration is included in the chapter’s hands-on steps, where an INI file named my_advanced_inventory. ini lists web1 and web2 and a db1 host. A common misconception is that INI cannot express complex structures; while true, INI remains useful for straightforward lists and quick manual edits. When you need nested dictionaries or lists as variables, YAML is a better choice. For practice, create an INI inventory and run a playbook that prints variables so you observe inline host overrides and the effect of [all:vars]. What will happen if a host has a host_vars file that defines the same variable?

keyIdea.title: INI is compact and explicit
keyIdea.text: Use INI for simple inventories and rely on inline host variables or [group:vars] for scoping when complexity is low.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › INI Format
INI Example
# INI format example: /etc/ansible/hosts
[webservers]
web1.example.com
web2.example.com

[databases]
db1.example.com ansible_port=2222
db2.example.com

[all:vars]
ansible_user=devops
ansible_ssh_private_key_file=/home/devops/.ssh/id_rsa
Note the inline host variable for db1.example.com. It overrides broader port settings.
Walkthrough & Tips
  • Brackets denote groups. Use [groupname:vars] for group-scoped variables.
  • Inline host variables set connection parameters per host.
  • INI is less suitable for nested complex data types.
Common mistake

Forgetting that a host_vars file will override inline host variables can lead to confusion; verify with inventory inspection commands when unsure.

Key Takeaway

INI works well for simple static lists and explicit inline host variables; use YAML when you need structure.

screens.title: Static Inventory: YAML Format
screens.narratorSegment: YAML inventories offer a structured and explicit hierarchy that becomes valuable when inventories contain nested variables or complex data types. The YAML example provided in the chapter shows an all top-level key, children groups, hosts nested under groups, and a vars section for global variables. The example demonstrates how db1. example. com can have an ansible_port key defined under its host mapping. Because YAML supports nested mappings and lists, it is easier to express dictionaries and other structured variables that would be awkward in INI. In practice, choose YAML when group variables are complex or when you want readable indentation and clearer relationships between groups and their hosts. A common pitfall is incorrect indentation; YAML is indentation-sensitive, so consistent spacing is essential. The hands-on activity suggests creating inventory. yml under your project directory, then running ansible-playbook with that inventory file. You can verify the resulting structure with ansible-inventory --list. Remember: both INI and YAML achieve the same end — a map of hosts and variables — but YAML scales better for data complexity. Try converting a small INI inventory to YAML to see where structure simplifies variable representation.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › YAML Format
YAML Example
# YAML format example: ~/ansible_projects/inventory.yml
all:
  children:
    webservers:
      hosts:
        web1.example.com:
        web2.example.com:
    databases:
      hosts:
        db1.example.com:
          ansible_port: 2222
        db2.example.com:
  vars:
    ansible_user: devops
    ansible_ssh_private_key_file: /home/devops/.ssh/id_rsa
YAML groups and vars read naturally, and nested host mappings let you attach dictionaries or lists easily.
Why choose YAML
  • Clear hierarchy for children and vars.
  • Better for structured variables and complex data.
  • Easier to maintain for larger inventories with nested definitions.
Common mistake

Incorrect indentation or mixing tabs and spaces will cause YAML parsing errors; validate files before use.

Key Takeaway

YAML gives you a readable, hierarchical inventory structure that's preferable for complex variables and nested data.

screens.title: Host Variables and Group Variables
screens.narratorSegment: Host variables apply to a single managed node and are used to override or extend values defined at broader scopes. Group variables apply to all members of a named group, making it easy to share configuration data among related hosts. The chapter explains common places to store these values: inside the inventory file itself, under group_vars/. yml, or host_vars/. yml. A typical use is to set http_port in group_vars/webservers. yml so every webserver uses that port; if one database host needs a different port, put ansible_port in host_vars/db1. example. com. yml. A concrete example from the hands-on activity shows a group_vars file that sets http_port and a host_vars file for db1 that overrides a welcome_message. One misconception is thinking group_vars will always be used even when a host file exists; host-specific files have higher precedence. Another practical note: file locations matter — Ansible loads group_vars and host_vars from the same directory as your inventory, so organizing inventory_dir with these folders keeps variable scope clear. Key takeaway: use group_vars for shared defaults and host_vars for targeted overrides, and when debugging, print variables to confirm which value is active.

keyIdea.text: Store shared defaults in group_vars and specific overrides in host_vars; Ansible loads these relative to the inventory location.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Host & Group Variables
Variable Locations
  • Inventory file inline or under group:vars / all:vars.
  • inventory_dir/group_vars/groupname.yml
  • inventory_dir/host_vars/hostname.yml
Example files
# group_vars/webservers.yml
---
http_port: 80
welcome_message: "Welcome to our web server!"

# host_vars/db1.example.com.yml
---
db_name: main_database
welcome_message: "Welcome to the database server!"
Behavior & Tips
  • Host variables override group or global variables for that host.
  • Keep variable files under inventory_dir so Ansible loads them automatically.
  • Use descriptive names and comments to avoid confusion during troubleshooting.
Pro tip

When testing precedence, use a display_vars playbook to print values and confirm which source provided each variable.

Key Takeaway

Group vars set defaults for many hosts; host vars are for specific overrides — organize them near the inventory for clarity.

screens.title: Variable Precedence in Ansible
screens.narratorSegment: Variable precedence determines which value Ansible uses when the same variable is defined in multiple places. The guideline is that definitions closer to the host override broader scope values. The chapter gives a clear practical example: a variable ansible_user defined in all:vars as devops but set in host_vars/web1. example. com. yml as webadmin — the host value webadmin is used for that host. Sources of variables include inventory, playbooks, roles, the command line, and more; while the chapter does not enumerate every precedence tier, it emphasizes the practical rule of thumb about specificity. A common error is assuming a global setting will always apply. When you see unexpected behavior, run ansible-inventory --list or use a debug task to print the variable so you can see which value is in effect. The provided assessment question reinforces this: with group_vars set to 100, host_vars set to 200, and all:vars set to 50, the effective value for the host is 200. When testing precedence, remember that facts and extra vars from the command line can also change resolution in real play runs, so always inspect the live resolved variables if results differ from expectations. What changed when you observe a different value than expected?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Variable Precedence
Precedence Example
Consider these definitions:
  • [all:vars] max_connections: 50
  • group_vars/webservers.yml max_connections: 100
  • host_vars/server1.example.com.yml max_connections: 200

Effective value for server1.example.com is 200 because host_vars take precedence over group and global vars.

Practical debugging

If a variable does not behave as expected, use inventory inspection and a debug play to print the resolved value. Extra vars passed on the command line can also override other sources, so include them in your checks.

Misconception

Believing group_vars always apply. In reality, more specific definitions — host_vars or command-line extra vars — take precedence.

Key Takeaway

Always check the specific scope where a variable is defined when results differ; specificity overrides broader defaults.

screens.title: Hands-on: Create an Advanced Static Inventory
screens.narratorSegment: The hands-on activity in this chapter walks you through creating a structured inventory directory and files. Start in your project folder and create my_advanced_inventory. ini, then add group_vars and host_vars directories. The INI example lists webservers and databases, and an all:vars section defines ansible_user and the SSH key path. Next create group_vars/webservers. yml to set http_port and a welcome_message that applies to web servers. Then create host_vars/db1. example. com. yml to set db_name and a welcome_message that will override the group message for that host. These steps demonstrate how local files provide both convenience and clarity when separating scoped variables. A practical tip: replace the example hostnames with actual hostnames or IP addresses for your environment. If you only have a single managed node, assign it to each necessary group to test different variable combinations. After creating the files, run the playbook to print variables and observe precedence; this live feedback is the fastest way to verify your structure. The process encourages disciplined inventory organization so you can scale and reason about variable origins as systems change. Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Create Inventory
Terminal Steps
cd ~/ansible_projects
nano my_advanced_inventory.ini
mkdir group_vars host_vars
# edit group_vars/webservers.yml and host_vars/db1.example.com.yml
Follow the sample content shown in other screens for the exact variable names used in playbook demonstrations.
Example INI snippet
# ~/ansible_projects/my_advanced_inventory.ini
[webservers]
web1.example.com
web2.example.com

[databases]
db1.example.com

[all:vars]
ansible_user=devops
ansible_ssh_private_key_file=/home/devops/.ssh/id_rsa
default_message="Hello from Ansible!"
Replace example hostnames with your targets. Use inventory-relative group_vars and host_vars.
Try this

keyIdea.title: Use playbooks to verify state
keyIdea.text: A simple playbook that prints variables is the fastest way to confirm how Ansible resolves values at runtime.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › display_vars Playbook
Playbook content
---
- name: Display host and group variables
  hosts: all
  tasks:
    - name: Print variables
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: |
          Hostname: {{ inventory_hostname }}
          Ansible User: {{ ansible_user }}
          Default Message: {{ default_message }}
          HTTP Port (if webserver): {{ http_port | default('N/A') }}
          DB Name (if database): {{ db_name | default('N/A') }}
          Welcome Message: {{ welcome_message }}
Note the use of default filters so missing values display as N/A rather than causing an error.
Run & Observe
Execute: ansible-playbook -i my_advanced_inventory.ini display_vars.yml and compare output for each host to the file definitions. Look for where welcome_message differs to see host override.
Common mistake

Expecting files to match runtime values without running the playbook. Always verify with a live run when troubleshooting precedence.

Key Takeaway

A debug playbook is a lightweight, reliable way to inspect resolved variables and confirm inventory behavior.

screens.title: Why Dynamic Inventory?
screens.narratorSegment: Dynamic inventory automates the discovery of hosts by querying an external source at runtime and returning YAML or JSON that Ansible can use as its inventory. The chapter highlights three practical benefits: accuracy, scalability, and flexibility. Accuracy means the inventory reflects the current set of running instances, avoiding stale entries. Scalability allows you to manage hundreds or thousands of hosts without manually editing files. Flexibility comes from grouping hosts by metadata such as tags or regions, often exposed by cloud providers. A key example is a cloud where instances start and stop frequently; a dynamic plugin can return only running instances filtered by state so your playbooks target the correct machines. The chapter also cautions that dynamic inventory needs secure credential handling — never hardcode A P I keys into inventory files. For the RHCE exam you may not configure cloud providers, but understanding dynamic inventory lets you reason about real-world automation where hosts are ephemeral. A simple thought exercise: in your current environment, what metadata would you want used to group hosts automatically? Answering that helps design the plugin configuration you might later use.

Benefits

  • Scalability: no manual updates for many hosts.
  • Flexibility: group by tags, regions, or other metadata.
Security note

Keep credentials out of inventory files. Use environment variables or secure stores where possible when configuring plugins.

Example use case

A cloud environment where instances are launched for autoscaling can be queried by a plugin that returns only instances in the running state and groups them by Environment or Role tags for targeted playbook runs.

Key Takeaway

Dynamic inventory keeps your automation aligned with reality — it discovers hosts and groups them from external metadata instead of relying on manual updates.

screens.title: Example: aws_ec2 Inventory Plugin

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › aws_ec2 Plugin
Plugin config example
# ~/ansible_projects/aws_ec2.yml
plugin: aws_ec2
regions:
  - us-east-1
filters:
  instance-state-name: running
keyed_groups:
  - key: tags.Environment
    prefix: env_
  - key: tags.Role
    prefix: role_
This config instructs the aws_ec2 plugin to return running instances in us-east-1 and create groups based on tags.
How to use

Run: ansible-playbook -i ~/ansible_projects/aws_ec2.yml playbook.yml. Or inspect generated inventory with: ansible-inventory -i ~/ansible_projects/aws_ec2.yml --list

Security reminder

Avoid placing credentials in this file. Use environment credentials or a secure credential provider for the plugin to use at runtime.

Key Takeaway

Inventory plugins create live inventories from external sources and can group hosts by metadata like tags for targeted automation.

screens.title: Inspecting Resolved Variables
screens.narratorSegment: Verifying resolved variables is an essential troubleshooting skill. The chapter recommends two complementary techniques: using ansible-inventory --list to see the structure generated by static or dynamic sources, and running a small debug playbook that prints variables at runtime. ansible-inventory --list outputs the inventory as JSON, making it easier to inspect group membership and variable keys. The debug playbook prints the actual values applied to each host during a playbook run, showing the effect of precedence. A typical workflow: after editing inventory or variable files, run ansible-inventory --list to confirm groups and host entries, then run your debug playbook to see the resolved variables in action. If a value is unexpected, check for host_vars files or extra vars passed on the command line that may override earlier definitions. The chapter warns that relying only on static file inspection can be misleading when using dynamic plugins — always run ansible-inventory when a plugin is in play. Practically, this approach shortens the time to diagnose variable conflicts and ensures your automation runs with the values you intend. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. screens.title: Security and Practical Notes for Dynamic Inventory
screens.narratorSegment: When using dynamic inventory, a critical consideration is how the plugin authenticates to the external source. The chapter advises against hardcoding credentials into inventory configuration files. Instead, prefer environment-based credential providers, native SDK credential chains, or a secured secrets store so credentials are not stored in plain text alongside inventory configuration. Another practical note is to filter returned instances so your inventory contains only the hosts you intend to manage, for example by filtering on instance-state-name: running. This reduces the chance of targeting terminated or stopped instances. Grouping by tags such as Environment or Role helps keep targeting precise, and it also makes playbooks easier to write because logical groups reflect your operational intent. For RHCE exam scenarios you may not configure cloud plugins, but these practices are important in production settings. A reflective question: how would you ensure your dynamic inventory never exposes credentials accidentally in a repository or logs? The answer usually involves not storing keys in files under version control and relying on runtime credential management instead. Credential safety
  • Avoid hardcoding API keys in inventory files.
  • Use environment variables, SDK credential chains, or a secrets store.

Filter and group carefully

Filter on instance-state-name: running to avoid terminated instances and use keyed_groups to group by tags so playbooks target intended hosts.

First, a static inventory is a manually created file in INI or YAML format; INI is compact while YAML is better for nested data. Second, variables can be scoped at host, group, or global levels. Host variables override group variables, which override global inventory variables. Third, dynamic inventory uses plugins or scripts to query external sources like cloud providers, returning an up-to-date set of hosts and metadata. Finally, ask yourself which inventory approach fits your current infrastructure and how you would secure credentials if you adopt dynamic inventories.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how Ansible discovers and organizes your managed nodes, why inventories matter, and how to move from small static lists to dynamic discovery. Inventories are the source of truth for Ansible. We will show you the two common static formats, INI and YAML, how to attach host and group variables so playbooks behave differently per machine, and how variable precedence resolves conflicts when multiple definitions exist. You will also see why dynamic inventories become essential in cloud environments where instances appear and disappear. A concrete example will walk through creating a structured inventory directory with group_vars and host_vars, then running a small playbook that prints resolved variables so you can observe precedence in action. Finally, we will examine a simple dynamic inventory plugin configuration for cloud discovery, and a safety note about securing credentials. By the end you should be able to choose a suitable inventory approach, locate where variables are defined, and diagnose unexpected variable values. Consider how having accurate inventory data could save time when you scale or troubleshoot automation.

These learning objectives map to hands-on skills you will practice. First, you will configure static Ansible inventory files using both INI and YAML formats so you can choose the right format for your environment. The INI form is quick and readable for small lists, while YAML supports nested data and clearer hierarchy. Second, you will define and use host and group variables to customize task behavior per machine or per group. You will learn where to place host_vars and group_vars files and why they matter. Third, you will understand Ansible's variable precedence — how conflicting definitions resolve — and practice diagnosing surprises using inventory and debug commands. Fourth, you will learn what a dynamic inventory is, why it is useful for cloud environments, and how to run a simple plugin or script to generate inventory automatically. Each objective is paired with a short competence milestone so you can verify you have mastered the skill. By the end, you should be able to choose a static versus dynamic approach, structure variables correctly, and explain why a host-specific value might override a global one.

These next objectives focus on practical verification and safe practices. You will learn to inspect resolved inventory data using Ansible commands so you can validate which variables are active at runtime. A common debugging pattern is to print variables with the debug module, which helps reveal when a host variable is overriding a group value. You will also practice creating a directory structure that separates inventory files from group_vars and host_vars so your configuration is maintainable. Finally, you will understand a safety checklist for dynamic inventories: do not hardcode A P I keys into inventory files, and ensure credentials are managed securely. A concrete example in this chapter walks through creating an aws_ec2 inventory configuration that queries running instances and groups them by tags. By the end you will be able to not only write inventories but also verify and secure them so they remain reliable as your infrastructure changes.

An Ansible inventory is the file or set of files that tell Ansible which machines to manage and how to reach them. At its core an inventory lists hosts, groups them logically, and can attach variables that change playbook behavior. Think of it as a directory and profile system combined: each host is listed and may have a profile made of variables. Static inventories are manually maintained files and are suitable for small or stable infrastructures. They provide control and predictability but become a burden when hosts are frequently created or removed. Dynamic inventories solve that by querying an external source at runtime. A useful mental model is to imagine static inventory as a phonebook you update by hand and dynamic inventory as a live directory that reads from the company's cloud account. A common misconception is to treat inventory only as a list of hostnames; in reality it is also the place where you attach host-specific or group-specific settings that playbooks consume. Example: when you add ansible_user in an all:vars section, that value applies broadly unless a host_vars file defines a different user for a single host. The key takeaway is that inventory controls both discovery and configuration context, so changes to inventory directly affect playbook execution and remote connections. How would your current workflow change if the inventory were always up-to-date?

The INI format is a long-standing, compact way to define static Ansible inventories. It uses bracketed group names, one host per line, and optional inline host variables. It’s ideal for quick setups or environments where nested data is minimal. The example in the chapter shows typical sections: a webservers group, a databases group with a host-specific ansible_port override, and an all:vars section for global variables. Practice reading inline variables carefully: a host line like db1. example. com ansible_port=2222 sets a host-level port that takes precedence over a group or all:vars value. You can also define group-level variables using [groupname:vars] which apply to members of that group. A concrete demonstration is included in the chapter’s hands-on steps, where an INI file named my_advanced_inventory. ini lists web1 and web2 and a db1 host. A common misconception is that INI cannot express complex structures; while true, INI remains useful for straightforward lists and quick manual edits. When you need nested dictionaries or lists as variables, YAML is a better choice. For practice, create an INI inventory and run a playbook that prints variables so you observe inline host overrides and the effect of [all:vars]. What will happen if a host has a host_vars file that defines the same variable?

YAML inventories offer a structured and explicit hierarchy that becomes valuable when inventories contain nested variables or complex data types. The YAML example provided in the chapter shows an all top-level key, children groups, hosts nested under groups, and a vars section for global variables. The example demonstrates how db1. example. com can have an ansible_port key defined under its host mapping. Because YAML supports nested mappings and lists, it is easier to express dictionaries and other structured variables that would be awkward in INI. In practice, choose YAML when group variables are complex or when you want readable indentation and clearer relationships between groups and their hosts. A common pitfall is incorrect indentation; YAML is indentation-sensitive, so consistent spacing is essential. The hands-on activity suggests creating inventory. yml under your project directory, then running ansible-playbook with that inventory file. You can verify the resulting structure with ansible-inventory --list. Remember: both INI and YAML achieve the same end — a map of hosts and variables — but YAML scales better for data complexity. Try converting a small INI inventory to YAML to see where structure simplifies variable representation.

Host variables apply to a single managed node and are used to override or extend values defined at broader scopes. Group variables apply to all members of a named group, making it easy to share configuration data among related hosts. The chapter explains common places to store these values: inside the inventory file itself, under group_vars/. yml, or host_vars/. yml. A typical use is to set http_port in group_vars/webservers. yml so every webserver uses that port; if one database host needs a different port, put ansible_port in host_vars/db1. example. com. yml. A concrete example from the hands-on activity shows a group_vars file that sets http_port and a host_vars file for db1 that overrides a welcome_message. One misconception is thinking group_vars will always be used even when a host file exists; host-specific files have higher precedence. Another practical note: file locations matter — Ansible loads group_vars and host_vars from the same directory as your inventory, so organizing inventory_dir with these folders keeps variable scope clear. Key takeaway: use group_vars for shared defaults and host_vars for targeted overrides, and when debugging, print variables to confirm which value is active.

Variable precedence determines which value Ansible uses when the same variable is defined in multiple places. The guideline is that definitions closer to the host override broader scope values. The chapter gives a clear practical example: a variable ansible_user defined in all:vars as devops but set in host_vars/web1. example. com. yml as webadmin — the host value webadmin is used for that host. Sources of variables include inventory, playbooks, roles, the command line, and more; while the chapter does not enumerate every precedence tier, it emphasizes the practical rule of thumb about specificity. A common error is assuming a global setting will always apply. When you see unexpected behavior, run ansible-inventory --list or use a debug task to print the variable so you can see which value is in effect. The provided assessment question reinforces this: with group_vars set to 100, host_vars set to 200, and all:vars set to 50, the effective value for the host is 200. When testing precedence, remember that facts and extra vars from the command line can also change resolution in real play runs, so always inspect the live resolved variables if results differ from expectations. What changed when you observe a different value than expected?

The hands-on activity in this chapter walks you through creating a structured inventory directory and files. Dynamic inventory automates the discovery of hosts by querying an external source at runtime and returning YAML or JSON that Ansible can use as its inventory. The chapter highlights three practical benefits: accuracy, scalability, and flexibility. Accuracy means the inventory reflects the current set of running instances, avoiding stale entries. Scalability allows you to manage hundreds or thousands of hosts without manually editing files. Flexibility comes from grouping hosts by metadata such as tags or regions, often exposed by cloud providers. A key example is a cloud where instances start and stop frequently; a dynamic plugin can return only running instances filtered by state so your playbooks target the correct machines. The chapter also cautions that dynamic inventory needs secure credential handling — never hardcode A P I keys into inventory files. For the RHCE exam you may not configure cloud providers, but understanding dynamic inventory lets you reason about real-world automation where hosts are ephemeral. A simple thought exercise: in your current environment, what metadata would you want used to group hosts automatically? Answering that helps design the plugin configuration you might later use.

A practical point: this approach eliminates manual host entries and automatically reflects the actual state of the cloud account. Verifying resolved variables is an essential troubleshooting skill. The chapter recommends two complementary techniques: using ansible-inventory --list to see the structure generated by static or dynamic sources, and running a small debug playbook that prints variables at runtime. ansible-inventory --list outputs the inventory as JSON, making it easier to inspect group membership and variable keys. The debug playbook prints the actual values applied to each host during a playbook run, showing the effect of precedence. A typical workflow: after editing inventory or variable files, run ansible-inventory --list to confirm groups and host entries, then run your debug playbook to see the resolved variables in action. If a value is unexpected, check for host_vars files or extra vars passed on the command line that may override earlier definitions. The chapter warns that relying only on static file inspection can be misleading when using dynamic plugins — always run ansible-inventory when a plugin is in play. Practically, this approach shortens the time to diagnose variable conflicts and ensures your automation runs with the values you intend. When using dynamic inventory, a critical consideration is how the plugin authenticates to the external source. The chapter advises against hardcoding credentials into inventory configuration files. Instead, prefer environment-based credential providers, native SDK credential chains, or a secured secrets store so credentials are not stored in plain text alongside inventory configuration. Another practical note is to filter returned instances so your inventory contains only the hosts you intend to manage, for example by filtering on instance-state-name: running. This reduces the chance of targeting terminated or stopped instances. Grouping by tags such as Environment or Role helps keep targeting precise, and it also makes playbooks easier to write because logical groups reflect your operational intent. For RHCE exam scenarios you may not configure cloud plugins, but these practices are important in production settings. These key concepts summarize what you should retain. First, a static inventory is a manually created file in INI or YAML format; INI is compact while YAML is better for nested data. Second, variables can be scoped at host, group, or global levels. Host variables override group variables, which override global inventory variables. Third, dynamic inventory uses plugins or scripts to query external sources like cloud providers, returning an up-to-date set of hosts and metadata. Keep credentials for dynamic inventory secure and prefer environment-based providers rather than hardcoding keys. Keep three compact ideas in mind. First, static inventories are simple and come in INI and YAML flavors; YAML is preferred when you need nested data. Second, variables live in inventory, group_vars, and host_vars; the most specific scope takes precedence. Third, dynamic inventory plugins query external services to produce an up-to-date inventory, which is powerful for cloud deployments but requires secure credential handling.
